report:
## Report

Evidence supports "yes, but cautiously" — honey appears modestly beneficial for acute cough in children over one year old, based on low-to-moderate certainty evidence.

The most authoritative source is the Cochrane systematic review (Oduwole et al.), which pooled randomized controlled trials comparing honey to placebo, no treatment, or over-the-counter cough medicines in children aged 1–18. It found honey may reduce cough frequency and severity better than no treatment/placebo and may outperform diphenhydramine, while showing no significant difference from dextromethorphan. However, the Cochrane team rated the underlying evidence as low quality due to small trial sizes, short follow-up (often just one night), and heterogeneity, so they stopped short of a strong recommendation (https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD007094.pub5/full; https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD007094_honey-acute-cough-children).

A 2023 updated systematic review in the European Journal of Pediatrics, incorporating four additional trials, reached a similar conclusion: low-quality evidence that honey is more effective than placebo/no treatment or cough medication for symptom relief and sleep improvement (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10570220/).

Individual trials reinforce this: a JAMA Pediatrics study found honey outperformed no treatment and performed comparably to dextromethorphan for nocturnal cough and sleep quality, while noting diphenhydramine and dextromethorphan were not superior to placebo (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapediatrics/fullarticle/571638).

Importantly, honey should never be given to infants under 12 months due to botulism risk (https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/honey-botulism.html).

**Conclusion:** Honey likely helps somewhat with acute cough symptoms in children over one, but evidence quality is low, effects are modest, and it's unsafe for infants under one year.
